prompts.concept: Neighbor-Joining scores every pair by Q before it joins. The closest pair in the matrix is the tempting first pick — does NJ join it first? Pick a cell in the matrix, or click two leaves.
prompts.math: NJ joins the pair minimizing Q(i,j) = (n-2)·d(i,j) - R_i - R_j. Each cluster's total distance to everything else counts, not just the pair's own distance.
prompts.reveal: The two orangutans — Pongo_pygmaeus and Pongo_abelii — join first under Q, even though the closest pair in the matrix is Pan_troglodytes and Pan_paniscus: the orangutans sit far enough from everything else that their Q wins. The trace on MEGA's printed matrix joins the same pair first, and the finished tree matches MEGA's split for split.

prompts.concept: The tree is complete — an unrooted NJ tree on the JC69 matrix. Read it by its splits: the two chimpanzees together, the two orangutans together, the African apes together — and the gibbon outside every grouping.
prompts.math: Every internal edge of an unrooted tree defines a split; two trees are the same tree exactly when their split sets match. The handout's next step re-runs this under K80 — on this data the model moves every distance but the same splits come back.

lab.title: MEGA: JC69 vs K2P on primate mtDNA
objectives: Run MEGA's distance → NJ chain under Jukes-Cantor and Kimura 2-parameter on a 7-taxon D-loop alignment
Match each MEGA analysis option to the NeoPhylo control that reproduces it
See where a transition-aware model changes the distances — and whether it changes the tree's splits
lab.handout_md:
## What this lab reproduces

The classic first MEGA distance chain: a pairwise-distance matrix under the Jukes-Cantor model, a Neighbor-Joining tree on it, then the same two runs under the Kimura 2-parameter model — every option set as the settings table lists it, so the numbers you reproduce are MEGA's own, recorded from MEGA-CC 12.1.4.

## The data

Seven hominoid sequences — human, the two chimpanzees, gorilla, the two orangutans and the gibbon — over 1,138 aligned sites of the mitochondrial control region (D-loop). The taxa come from the same public records (Horai et al., 1995) as MEGA's own example data; this alignment is the bundled `primate-mtdna` library dataset, covering that control region only — do not expect MEGA's own example file to print these numbers.

To cross-check in MEGA itself: load this lab, export the alignment as `.meg` from NeoPhylo's Export menu, open that file in MEGA, and apply the settings table exactly — the distance run first, then the NJ tree, for each model.

## Before you start

Read the settings table. In MEGA each run's options live in the analysis dialog you reach from the menu path in the second column; the table lists every option the runs set — nothing is left to a default — next to the NeoPhylo control that reproduces it.

## Steps

1. Load this lab. NeoPhylo loads the alignment and computes the JC69 matrix — the first run's model — under pairwise deletion, MEGA's default gap treatment.
2. Look at the matrix before the tree. Which pair looks closest? Write your prediction down — NJ does not always join the closest pair first.
3. Step through the joins and read the finished tree as unrooted: which splits does it contain?
4. Switch the Correction control to K80 — MEGA's "Kimura 2-parameter" — and recompute: the second MEGA run. Which cells changed?
5. Build the tree again under K80 and compare its splits with the JC69 run's.

## Questions

- K2P scores transitions and transversions separately; JC69 treats all substitutions alike. Did the model change every distance on this data, and which pair's distance moved most? What does the direction of the change say about this alignment?
- Did the model change the tree's splits here? On what kind of data would you expect it to?
- In the sandbox, switch the gap treatment to Complete deletion: how many columns does this alignment lose, and does the closest pair change?
- MEGA's matrix prints to 8 decimals; NeoPhylo's cells show 3. Where do the extra decimals actually matter — in reading the matrix, or in the tree built on it?

lab.mega_note_md:
MEGA's distance output is a lower-triangle text matrix — one row per added taxon, every cell printed to 8 decimals, with `n/c` where a distance cannot be estimated (not an issue here: every pair of the seven sequences has comparable sites). NeoPhylo draws the full square matrix as a heatmap: cells read to 3 decimals on screen, and a cell that cannot be estimated shows ∞.

MEGA's inferred tree opens in the Tree Explorer as a drawn phylogram with branch lengths. NeoPhylo draws the same unrooted tree as computed — compare the splits, not the direction a drawing happens to grow from — and its Newick export carries the computed branch lengths (MEGA's `.nwk` prints them at up to 16 decimals).

One naming detail worth knowing: MEGA's "Kimura 2-parameter model" is the K80 formula — the correction NeoPhylo calls K80. The `K2P_PHYLIP` correction looks similar but reproduces PHYLIP dnadist's fixed-ratio estimator instead, so it does not match MEGA.
